_note: Worked example corpus for recall_extender.py --corpus (post-submission addition, 2026-07-23). 13 short documents across two collider-safety-debate communities, built ONLY from text already committed in this repo under demo-collider/ -- the paragraph-level usage excerpts at demo-collider/cross-side/excerpts/*.txt and demo-collider/term-check/.term-check/prompts/*-excerpts.txt (both committed; the full third-party paper texts they were pulled from are NOT committed, per demo-collider/README.md's copyright boundary). Every 'text' below is a VERBATIM substring of one of those committed excerpt files -- split at sentence boundaries into shorter passages, with inline math rendered to plain ASCII per the excerpts' own stated convention ('inline formulae rendered to ASCII'), and with '[...]' left in place wherever an intervening sentence was skipped, exactly as the source excerpt files already mark cuts. Nothing here was paraphrased, generated, or invented. This is a DEMONSTRATION corpus for the recall-extender interface, not a new research measurement -- see prototype/example-owndata/README.md and prototype/README.md's dated 2026-07-23 section for the honesty scope that applies to any run on this data.

documents.source: Giddings & Mangano 2008 (arXiv:0806.3381), Sec 4.1 'Accretion basics' -- verbatim, via demo-collider/cross-side/excerpts/A1-accretion-mechanism.txt
documents.text: Our interest is in accretion of black holes trapped inside astronomical bodies such as planets, stars, neutron stars, etc. One parameter governing this accretion is the effective capture radius r_c(M) of the black hole, for a given mass. This is the radius out to which the gravitational field of the black hole succeeds in attracting matter that will eventually be absorbed.

documents.source: Giddings & Mangano 2008 (arXiv:0806.3381), Sec 4.1 'Accretion basics' -- verbatim, via demo-collider/cross-side/excerpts/A1-accretion-mechanism.txt
documents.text: The other parameter is the flux of mass towards the black hole, F. Specifically, the black hole mass grows as dM/dt = pi r_c^2 F. [...] The capture radius r_c is frequently different from the Schwarzschild radius R, and depends on the size and state of motion of the black hole, as well as on properties of the surrounding medium.

documents.source: Giddings & Mangano 2008 (arXiv:0806.3381), Sec 2.1 'Instability of microscopic black holes' -- verbatim, via demo-collider/cross-side/excerpts/A2-hawking-decay.txt
documents.text: One of the most profound steps so far towards the yet-incomplete unification of quantum mechanical and gravitational principles was Hawking's discovery that black holes evaporate. This provided an important missing link in the pre-existing laws of black hole thermodynamics, by explicitly calculating the temperature that characterizes a radiating black hole.

documents.source: Giddings & Mangano 2008 (arXiv:0806.3381), Sec 2.1 'Instability of microscopic black holes' -- verbatim, via demo-collider/cross-side/excerpts/A2-hawking-decay.txt
documents.text: Belief in the robustness of Hawking's prediction of nearly thermal evaporation has been boosted by arguments for the result which have now been produced from several different directions. These derivations have the virtue of either facing head-on the issue of the transplanckian modes, or being independent of them, and the basic effect has survived a number of important consistency checks.

documents.source: Giddings & Mangano 2008 (arXiv:0806.3381), side-A prose -- verbatim, via demo-collider/term-check/.term-check/prompts/20260721T013948Z-accretion-slow-down-excerpts.txt
documents.text: Collisions can slow such a black hole via two mechanisms. First, in a typical collision the black hole will gravitationally scatter a particle in its asymptotic field, thus losing some of its momentum. We henceforth refer to this gravitational mechanism as Coulomb slow-down.

documents.source: Giddings & Mangano 2008 (arXiv:0806.3381), side-A prose -- verbatim, via demo-collider/term-check/.term-check/prompts/20260721T013948Z-accretion-slow-down-excerpts.txt
documents.text: Second, for smaller impact parameters, a black hole can absorb a particle, in the process possibly emitting some radiation, and typically increasing its mass. This also slows the black hole, and will be referred to as accretion slow-down.

documents.source: Giddings & Mangano 2008 (arXiv:0806.3381), Sec 7.4 'Summary of white dwarf constraints' -- verbatim, via demo-collider/cross-side/excerpts/B1-wd-survival-bound.txt
documents.text: This and the preceding sections have argued that in the hypothetical TeV-scale gravity scenarios possibly relevant to LHC, 1) cosmic rays will produce significant numbers of black holes on white dwarfs of low (few x 10^5 G) magnetic fields, on time scales short as compared to known white dwarf lifetimes; 2) such black holes, even if neutral and with the highest masses accessible at the LHC, will be stopped on white dwarfs with masses M >~ M_sun, by accreting and scattering the dense matter of the star during their transit; and 3) the white dwarf will then be accreted.

documents.source: Giddings & Mangano 2008 (arXiv:0806.3381), Sec 7.4 'Summary of white dwarf constraints' -- verbatim, via demo-collider/cross-side/excerpts/B1-wd-survival-bound.txt
documents.text: Accretion of a white dwarf has been argued to be more rapid than that of Earth. [...] Second, white dwarfs pack the mass of the Sun into a region the size of the Earth, so are much more dense, and have much higher internal pressures, assisting accretion. [...] The above arguments thus state that comparison of respective accretion rates, together with survival of white dwarfs to observed time scales >~ 10^8 years, implies survival of Earth for a significantly longer time, and in particular longer than the natural solar lifetime.

documents.source: Giddings & Mangano 2008 (arXiv:0806.3381), Sec 2.2 'Cosmic ray collisions on Earth' -- verbatim, via demo-collider/cross-side/excerpts/B2-cosmic-ray-survival.txt
documents.text: Cosmic rays hit Earth with energies known to exceed 10^20 eV, corresponding to center-of-mass (CM) energies exceeding 100 TeV. Thus, anything that can be made with Earth-based accelerators up to this energy is already being made by nature.

documents.source: Giddings & Mangano 2008 (arXiv:0806.3381), Sec 2.2 'Cosmic ray collisions on Earth' -- verbatim, via demo-collider/cross-side/excerpts/B2-cosmic-ray-survival.txt
documents.text: This argument can be used to effectively rule out the existence of particles predicted by some speculative scenarios, or to exclude possible macroscopic consequences of high energy collisions, as discussed for example in the literature. This argument requires however more attention if the large momentum imparted to the produced particles by the cosmic-ray kinematics has an impact on how they evolve after production.

documents.source: Giddings & Mangano 2008 (arXiv:0806.3381), side-B prose (neutron-star crossover) -- verbatim, math rendered to ASCII, via demo-collider/term-check/.term-check/prompts/20260721T014110Z-macroscopic-absorption-excerpts.txt
documents.text: Like in atomic matter, one might expect different phases for black hole accretion within a NS, depending on the relative range of the black hole's influence as compared to the radii R_D, R_C representing crossover to lower-dimensional behavior, and as compared to 1 fm, the characteristic separation between nucleons, which delineates the crossover from microscopic to macroscopic absorption in the NS context.

documents.source: Giddings & Mangano 2008 (arXiv:0806.3381), side-B prose (neutron-star crust bound) -- verbatim, math rendered to ASCII, via demo-collider/term-check/.term-check/prompts/20260721T014256Z-crust-penetration-time-excerpts.txt
documents.text: The mean free path d_free reaches a minimum near the bottom of the crust, and consequently the average velocity is slowest there.

documents.source: Giddings & Mangano 2008 (arXiv:0806.3381), side-B prose (neutron-star crust bound) -- verbatim, math rendered to ASCII, via demo-collider/term-check/.term-check/prompts/20260721T014256Z-crust-penetration-time-excerpts.txt
documents.text: We can therefore bound the crust penetration time by using rho = m_p / fm^3 to derive a minimum gravitational drift velocity and time.
